input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The change happened on April ninth, after the building manager finished replacing a loose floor tile and painted a yellow line around the new shelf area. The lending group had eleven regular volunteers and about eighty games at the time, and we wanted visitors to find the games without walking through a class in progress. I am describing the move because the forwarding of one note became important to how we handled the first month of the new arrangement.

Before the move, Elian Cruz kept the paper sign-out sheet in a green folder and tracked overdue games on a small calendar. He said, “People ask where the shelf is even when they can see it from the desk.” The new alcove faced the reception counter, but a tall plant partly blocked the view from the main door. We moved the plant to the window on the following Monday and left a strip of blue tape on the floor to show where visitors could stand while reading the rules. The tape was not meant to mark a queue, and the sign said that in plain language near the bottom.

Our shelf rules allowed each household to borrow two games for fourteen days. A household could request one extra week if nobody else had reserved either game. Returned pieces had to be counted at the table rather than in the hallway because dice and tokens had previously rolled under the radiator. The shelf was open whenever the building was open, except during the Thursday after-school club, when the alcove served as a quiet room. Volunteers still took returns at the desk then and placed them in the red tray until the club ended.

1. The blue binder holds the sign-out sheets and the list of volunteer shifts.
2. The red tray is only for returned games that need a piece check.
3. The yellow card beside the shelf has the reservation instructions and the library phone number.
4. The small black box contains spare pencils and blank return slips.

Elian made this list for the new volunteers after two visitors put completed slips inside the binder and one volunteer stored a returned game in the pencil box. The list stayed inside the cabinet door rather than on the public notice board because it included the phone number for the volunteer lead.

On April seventeenth, a family brought back Foxes at Dusk with one wooden marker missing. They had borrowed it on opening day and returned it in the red tray with a note saying that the marker might be inside the cloth bag. The game was not reserved, so the volunteer on duty could wait until the next shift to check every piece. If it had been reserved for that afternoon, she would have called the family before lending it again. That condition mattered because the reservation card only showed the game title and the first name of the next borrower.

The volunteer checked the box under the game insert and found the marker caught in a folded corner. The family had also left a small paper map they had drawn to show where they found the loose pieces. The map was not part of the game and was returned to them on their next visit. Elian wrote the repair date on the inside inventory card and left the reservation card unchanged. The same afternoon, two people asked whether the game could be held past closing, and the volunteer explained that a reservation did not extend the building hours.

On April twentieth, I was asked to forward the shelf group's note about the new location to the neighborhood bulletin editor. I used the address from the contact sheet and forwarded the note before the evening shift began. The note said the shelf had moved to the east alcove and listed the hours and borrowing limit. It also asked readers to bring games back with all their pieces and to use the red tray for returns that needed checking. Elian said, “Please keep the last line about the Thursday club because it saves a trip for families.” I kept that line in the note.

The editor replied the next morning and said the bulletin would run on Friday, but that the map needed a shorter label. She asked whether “east entrance alcove” was the approved location wording, and I checked with the building manager before answering. He confirmed that the public directory called the place the east alcove and that the entrance phrase could make people look for a separate room. I replied with the directory wording, and the editor sent back a proof that afternoon. The group had no request to change the lending rules, so the proof only changed the location label and the order of the contact details.

At the end of April, we counted seventy-six games on the shelf and four in the red tray. Two needed replacement pieces, and one had a reservation waiting for Saturday. The volunteer lead taped a fresh copy of the hours beside the yellow card because the old copy had curled near the radiator. The plant stayed beside the window, and the blue floor strip stayed in place. We kept the green folder at the reception desk and continued using the paper sheets while the group discussed whether to make a digital list. Nobody had approved a change to the sign-out process.

The first month in the alcove went smoothly, but the group still had small jobs to finish. Elian planned to bring a ruler to check that the yellow card was level, and the volunteer lead wanted to ask the after-school staff whether the quiet room schedule would change in summer. We left both tasks on the next meeting agenda rather than guessing at an answer. Families continued to ask about the extra week, and volunteers pointed to the reservation rule on the card. The forward note remained in the bulletin file, and the editor's proof was clipped behind it for anyone who needed to confirm the published location."}]
